title: Short Stuff: Père-Lachaise Cemetery
summary: Short Stuff episode on Père-Lachaise Cemetery in Paris, one of the world's most famous cemeteries. The hosts discuss its origin in 1804 under Napoleon as a landscape-style cemetery departing from crowded medieval churchyards, its size (over 100 acres, more than a million interments), and its segregated-feeling sections. They cover Paris's cemetery shortage (about 5,000 requests for roughly 150 plots per year across fourteen city cemeteries), high plot prices, and famous burials including Jim Morrison, Oscar Wilde, Chopin, Édith Piaf, Marcel Proust, Marcel Marceau, Molière, Gertrude Stein, Sarah Bernhardt, Georges Seurat, Isadora Duncan, and Abelard and Héloïse. They explain the name comes from Père François de La Chaise, confessor to Louis XIV, and mention about four million annual visitors. The episode closes with a comparison to other cemeteries such as Oakland Cemetery in Atlanta and the Woodstock, New York cemetery with Levon Helm and Rick Danko's graves.
topics: Woodstock cemetery Levon Helm Rick Danko

segments.title: Opening banter and Jim Morrison
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the show, joking about Jim Morrison's nickname and noting that he is buried at Père-Lachaise.

segments.title: Chuck's visits to the cemetery
segments.summary: Chuck describes visiting the cemetery on trips to Paris and seeing trinkets and offerings at Morrison's grave.

segments.title: Origins and size of Père-Lachaise
segments.summary: The hosts describe how the cemetery began the landscape-garden cemetery style, opened in 1804 under Napoleon, and covers over 100 acres with more than a million interments.

segments.title: Neighborhoods and Paris cemetery demand
segments.summary: Chuck notes the cemetery's sections are divided by religion. Josh cites about 5,000 requests for roughly 150 annual plots across Paris's fourteen city cemeteries.

segments.title: Plot prices and buying a grave
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether plots can be bought, how demand raises prices, and joke about how plots become available.

segments.title: Famous people buried at the cemetery
segments.summary: Chuck lists graves he visited, including Oscar Wilde, Chopin, Édith Piaf, and Marcel Proust. Josh adds Marcel Marceau, and the hosts correct some misremembered names.

segments.title: Marcel Marceau and joking corrections
segments.summary: Josh jokingly describes a bust on Marceau's headstone, then admits he made it up. The hosts joke about a jazz cigarette from Morrison's grave.

segments.title: Molière and early relocation of famous remains
segments.summary: Josh explains that Molière's remains were moved to the new cemetery to draw attention. Chuck links this to ongoing burial space problems in Paris.

segments.title: Burial space, more names, and Isadora Duncan correction
segments.summary: The hosts discuss why plots ran out, mention Gertrude Stein and Sarah Bernhardt, and Josh corrects himself on Isadora Duncan and Gertrude Stein.

segments.title: Name origin: Père François de La Chaise
segments.summary: Josh explains the cemetery's name comes from Père François de La Chaise, confessor to Louis XIV, and that La Chaise means 'the chair' in French.

segments.title: Visitors and cemetery as urban park
segments.summary: Chuck describes the cemetery as a shady respite in the city, and the hosts say about four million people visit each year.

segments.title: Address and Abelard and Héloïse
segments.summary: Josh gives the cemetery's address on Rue du Repos and describes Abelard and Héloïse, whose letters are still read and whose remains were reburied together in a crypt.

segments.title: Other cemeteries: Hollywood Forever, Oakland, Woodstock
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether Short Stuff covered Hollywood Forever, mention Oakland Cemetery in Atlanta, and name the Woodstock, New York cemetery with Levon Helm and Rick Danko's graves.
topics: Woodstock cemetery Levon Helm Rick Danko

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck closes the short stuff episode, and the closing credits note the show is an iHeartRadio production.
